extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and practitioners interested in U.S. First Amendment law
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic summary of legal doctrines, tests, and precedents that define the scope and limits of First Amendment protections in the United States. Covers doctrines for campaign finance, schools, press, commercial speech, obscenity, assembly, association, and related categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaign finance speech / contribution limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaign donations are sometimes treated as speech protected by the First Amendment; limits on contributions can serve a governmental interest in safeguarding electoral integrity but also implicate speech rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buckley v. Valeo (1976) upheld contribution limits as serving the basic governmental interest in safeguarding the integrity of the electoral process while recognizing campaign finance as political speech. Citizens United v. FEC (2010) held restrictions on independent political spending by corporations or unions violated the Free Speech Clause, enabling outside groups to spend more on elections. McCutcheon v. FEC (2014) found federal aggregate donation limits to clash with the First Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional/occupational speech doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Some courts treated speech directed to individuals in a professional/fiduciary context as subject to different First Amendment rules (so-called 'professional speech').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Byron White (Lowe v. SEC, 1985) suggested government could restrict speech 'one who takes the affairs of a client personally in hand…in light of the client's individual needs.' Over time courts adopted a 'professional speech' view, but the Supreme Court repudiated it in National Institute of Family & Life Advocates v. Becerra (2018), stating the Court has never recognized 'professional speech' as a separate category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag desecration / expressive conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Burning or desecration of the U.S. flag as protest has been treated as expressive conduct subject to First Amendment protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Street v. New York (1969) left flag-burning constitutionality unaddressed; Texas v. Johnson (1989) explicitly ruled flag burnings are a form of protected speech. The issue remains the subject of intense debate but the Court has found flag desecration protected where not a direct personal insult.

rubrics_metrics.name: School-student speech: Tinker material-disruption test
rubrics_metrics.description: Students retain First Amendment rights at school, but those rights can be limited where speech materially and substantially interferes with school activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tinker v. Des Moines (1969): schools cannot restrict symbolic speech that does not 'materially and substantially' interrupt school activities. Subsequent cases have limited Tinker: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier (1988) allows restricting student speech inconsistent with a school's basic educational mission; Morse v. Frederick (2007) permits restriction of student speech at school-sponsored events that promote illegal drug use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional free-speech policies (campus statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: University or institutional free-speech policies seek to protect expression on campus and combat censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the University of Chicago's 'Chicago Statement' (2014) is a free speech policy designed to combat censorship on campus and has been adopted by other universities; institutional policies interact with court doctrines governing student speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelled speech prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: The First Amendment protects citizens from being compelled by the government to speak or to pay for certain speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette (1943) ruled schoolchildren cannot be punished for refusing to say the Pledge of Allegiance or salute the flag. Janus v. AFSCME (2018) held requiring a public-sector employee to pay union dues when not a member violated the First Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hate and offensive speech protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Offensive or hateful language, broadly defined, is generally protected by the First Amendment though difficult to define precisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court has recognized 'freedom for the thought we hate' (Holmes). The American Library Association defines hate speech as expression intended to vilify or incite hatred against protected groups. Snyder v. Phelps (2011) found highly offensive protest signs at a military funeral fell within First Amendment protection. Distinction: hate crimes (which stir criminal activity or threaten individuals) can be illegal even when the speech itself may be protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fighting words doctrine (limited category not protected)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal insults and deliberately violent statements directed at a particular person or group (fighting words) are not protected speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fighting words doctrine excludes 'personal insults and deliberately violent statements directed at a particular person or group' from protection — e.g., a 1940s conviction for insulting a police officer was upheld. The doctrine has been criticized as a 'relic' but remains a recognized limitation when speech constitutes direct personal affront likely to provoke immediate violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code as speech / source code doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer source code and similar digital expressions can be treated as expressive speech protected by the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bernstein v. United States (Ninth Circuit) held source code is a form of expressive language. The doctrine has been invoked in disputes over encryption export controls, the Apple-FBI case, and to argue protection for publishing/running software for cryptocurrencies, privacy tools, 3D-printed gun files, and DRM-bypass tools. The treatment of code as speech remains active litigation and scholarly debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial speech and the Central Hudson test
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial speech (aimed at selling a product or service) is entitled to First Amendment protection but less so than political speech; restrictions are evaluated under a four-part test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp. v. Public Service Commission (1980) developed a four-pronged test: (1) the speech must be legal and not misleading; (2) the government must have a substantial interest in regulating it; (3) the regulation must directly advance that interest; and (4) the regulation must not be more restrictive than necessary. The Court has noted 'speech does not lose its protection simply because money is transacted through it.' Posadas de Puerto Rico (1986) upheld advertising restrictions as preserving governmental interests (example: barring casinos from advertising).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation standards: actual malice and private-figure rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for libel/defamation depend on the plaintiff's status (public official/figure vs private individual) and whether statements are provably false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964) transformed U.S. libel law by requiring public officials (and later public figures) to prove 'actual malice' — knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth — by clear and convincing evidence. Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc. (1974) held private individuals need not show actual malice. Milkovich v. Lorain Journal Co. (1990) ruled the First Amendment does not create a wholesale opinion exception; statements labeled 'opinion' may be actionable if provably false. Historically, common-law libel emphasized result (harm) over truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity: Roth and Miller tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscene speech is not protected by the First Amendment; the Miller test establishes a three-part standard to determine obscenity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roth v. United States (1957) found obscenity outside First Amendment protection and originated standards. Miller v. California (1973) expanded the test: a work is obscene if (a) 'the average person, applying contemporary community standards' would find the work as a whole appeals to the prurient interest; (b) the work depicts sexual conduct in a patently offensive way as specifically defined by state law; and (c) the work, taken as a whole, lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. Justice Potter Stewart's 'I know it when I see it' (Jacobellis) encapsulates difficulties in definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child pornography exception to Miller
rubrics_metrics.description: Material involving child sexual exploitation is not governed by Miller and may be prohibited regardless of other tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York v. Ferber (1982) and Osborne v. Ohio (1990) held the government's interest in protecting children permits banning child pornography; the Miller test does not apply to child pornography prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private possession of obscene material in the home
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal possession of obscene material in the home may be constitutionally protected from prohibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stanley v. Georgia (1969) held that the state may not criminalize private possession of obscene material in the home, distinguishing possession from distribution or production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of the press and prior restraint standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Free Press Clause protects publication and dissemination of information; prior restraint (pre-publication censorship) is heavily disfavored and requires a very high burden to justify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Near v. Minnesota (1931) rejected prior restraint laws. New York Times Co. v. United States (1971) (Pentagon Papers) ruled the government had not met the heavy burden required for prior restraint; Justice Brennan explained only proof that publication will 'inevitably, directly, and immediately' cause a grave harm can justify prior restraint. The press is protected broadly across media; the Court has also recognized limits where national security or immediate risks are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press privilege and compelled publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The government generally cannot force media to publish material they do not wish to publish; claims for press privilege must be balanced against obligations to give relevant testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miami Herald Publishing Co. v. Tornillo (1974) struck down a law requiring newspapers to publish responses from criticized candidates, establishing a corporation's right not to speak. Branzburg v. Hayes (1972) held claims for press privilege must be judged on facts to balance freedom of the press with obligations of testimony in criminal conduct investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasting and scarcity regulation (content-neutral limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast media (television/radio) due to scarcity may be subject to content-neutral regulation not afforded to print media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Communications Commission v. Pacifica Foundation upheld FCC authority to restrict 'indecent' material in broadcasting. The Court has sustained greater regulation of broadcasters because of limited frequencies, but requires content-neutral application and scrutiny about suppression of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation and differential treatment of media
rubrics_metrics.description: States may tax media, but taxes targeting newspapers or that present a danger of suppressing particular ideas can violate the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grosjean v. American Press Co. (1936) found taxes focusing exclusively on newspapers unconstitutional. Leathers v. Medlock (1991) allowed treating different media types differently (e.g., taxing cable but not newspapers) unless the tax is directed at or threatens to suppress particular ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to petition and scope of petition clause
rubrics_metrics.description: The Petition Clause protects the right to petition the government for a redress of grievances and includes broader communications with government branches, lobbying, and litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The clause protects petitions to Congress, executive, and judiciary and includes lobbying and filing lawsuits. Petitions on behalf of private interests and those calling for peaceful legislative change are protected. Borough of Duryea v. Guarnieri (2011) declared the Free Speech Clause and Petition Clause mutually integral to democratic exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of assembly / public forum protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to peaceably assemble protects individuals' ability to come together to express, promote, and defend shared ideas and is applied broadly to public forums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An early case (United States v. Cruikshank, 1875) recognized assembly rights; Hague v. Committee for Industrial Organization (1939) held freedom of assembly applies to public forums like streets and parks; the right is deemed equally important as free speech and free press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of association and membership privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of association (though not explicit in the Amendment) is protected; privacy of membership and the ability to exclude members in some circumstances are components of the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NAACP v. Alabama (1958) held privacy of membership essential. Roberts v. United States Jaycees (1984) said associations may not exclude people for reasons unrelated to expression (e.g., gender), while Hurley v. Irish-American GLB Group of Boston (1995) allowed exclusion if presence would affect the group's ability to advocate a particular viewpoint. Boy Scouts of America v. Dale (2000) held that forcing admission of an openly gay member infringed the Boy Scouts' right to free association.
